figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overall architecture of OpenRLHF. The system assigns GPUs to two primary roles: rollout engines dedicated to response generation and actor engines responsible for computing log-probabilities and model training. OpenRLHF leverages Ray for distributed scheduling, integrates vLLM to achieve efficient response rollout with low GPU memory usage, and employs DeepSpeed ZeRO for 3D parallelism (including tensor, data, and sequence parallelism) to enable efficient training. The underlying models are instantiated with flexible Transformer architectures, making the system easy to extend and adapt for diverse scenarios.

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) fine-tuned via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) significantly improve the alignment of human-AI values, further raising the upper bound of AI capabilities, particularly in reasoning-intensive, long-context Chain-of-Thought (CoT) tasks. However, existing frameworks commonly face challenges such as inference bottlenecks and complexity barriers, which restrict their accessibility to newcomers. To bridge this gap, we introduce OpenRLHF, a user-friendly, scalable, and easy-to-learn open-source RLHF framework built upon Ray, vLLM, DeepSpeed, and HuggingFace Transformers, featuring a simplified design, clear code structure, and comprehensive documentation to facilitate entry for researchers and practitioners. Experimental results show that OpenRLHF achieves superior training efficiency, with speedups ranging from 1.22× to 1.68× across different model sizes, compared to state-of-the-art frameworks. Additionally, it requires significantly fewer lines of code for implementation. OpenRLHF is publicly available at https://github.com/OpenRLHF/OpenRLHF, and has already been adopted by leading institutions to accelerate RLHF research and learning.

sections.body: The introduction says RLHF and RLVR fine-tuning of LLMs improves alignment and reasoning, including long CoT outputs. It states that inference often accounts for over 90% of total RLHF or RLVR runtime, since models generate thousands of tokens per step. It reviews DeepSpeed-Chat, TRL, ColossalChat, Nemo-aligner, ChatLearn and verl, and says the industrial systems are tightly coupled, with steep learning curves. It lists OpenRLHF's contributions: a Ray-based architecture, 3D parallelism with DeepSpeed and ring attention, CoT inference with vLLM, and asynchronous dataflow. It reports adoption by CMU, MIT, Microsoft and HKUST.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: RLHF and RLVR training is dominated by inference cost, and existing frameworks are hard for newcomers to adopt.

sections.body: The related work section describes PPO as the dominant RLHF optimizer and DPO as a more computationally efficient alternative. It groups prior systems into general-purpose RL frameworks, which it says often fail on LLM-specific challenges, and RLHF-specific frameworks. Open-source options such as TRL, DeepSpeed-Chat and ColossalChat are described as accessible but weak at orchestration and inference optimization. Industrial options such as Nemo-aligner, ChatLearn and verl are described as offering advanced optimizations but requiring substantial engineering expertise. The section concludes that most frameworks address inference bottlenecks and usability poorly at the same time. This section reports no experiments.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior frameworks force a choice between high performance and ease of use.

sections.body: This section gives the system design. OpenRLHF assigns GPUs to two roles: a rollout engine that generates responses, using vLLM, and a ZeRO engine that computes log-probabilities and performs training, with Ray handling scheduling. Model training uses DeepSpeed for tensor, data and sequence parallelism. Ring attention provides sequence parallelism for long CoT workloads, and automatic tensor parallelism is applied to Hugging Face models by default. Asynchronous dataflow lets rollout, actor and remote engines run independently and exchange messages. Figure 1 summarizes the architecture.
sections.heading: Design of OpenRLHF
sections.headline: OpenRLHF assigns GPUs to rollout and training roles under Ray, with vLLM generating responses.

sections.body: The experiments compare OpenRLHF with verl on long-CoT RLVR training for 1.5B, 7B and 14B models at 1K to 8K generation lengths, on 8 NVIDIA H200 140GB GPUs. Table 1 reports per-step training time in seconds, with average speedups from 1.22× for 1.5B to 1.68× for 14B. A GSM8K run with GRPO for one epoch takes 1,657 seconds for OpenRLHF and 5,189 seconds for TRL, approximately 3.1×. A PPO run on 1,024 prompts takes 236.8 seconds for OpenRLHF and 855.09 seconds for DeepSpeed-Chat, a 3.6× speedup. The section credits vLLM and Ray for the DeepSpeed-Chat gain, and each comparison uses identical hyperparameter settings.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: OpenRLHF trains 1.22× to 1.68× faster than verl across three model sizes in Table 1.

sections.body: The limitations section states that OpenRLHF may not match peak performance of highly specialized industrial frameworks. As a community-driven project without dedicated economic support, it may integrate cutting-edge features more slowly than commercial frameworks. It primarily supports language models and does not support Vision-Language Models or other multimodal architectures. Its dependence on Ray, vLLM and DeepSpeed means upstream updates may need maintenance work or cause compatibility issues. The section still states that the accessibility contributions provide significant value to the community.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limitations include no multimodal support, possibly lower peak performance than industrial frameworks, and upstream dependency risk.

sections.body: The conclusion restates OpenRLHF as a framework that bridges performance and usability for RLHF and RLVR. It lists four innovations: a Ray-based architecture, 3D parallelism for scaling, accelerated CoT inference, and asynchronous dataflow. It cites adoption across leading institutions and companies, from CMU academic courses to production deployments, as validation of real-world effectiveness. It also says OpenRLHF has influenced subsequent frameworks. The authors state that open-sourcing the framework aims to accelerate research and broaden participation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion summarizes four design innovations and cites institutional adoption as validation.

sections.body: The appendix has three parts. Appendix A lists contributors by component, including Ray, vLLM, ring attention, DeepSpeed, GRPO, PPO and documentation. Appendix B lists adoption: a CMU course in Spring 2025, companies such as Google, ByteDance, Baidu and NVIDIA, and derivative frameworks LMM-R1, MARTI and MM-EUREKA. Appendix C describes the PPO workflow in four stages: rollout generation, reward computation, advantage estimation with GAE, and policy optimization with a clipped objective. Figure 3 shows this workflow.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists contributors, adopting institutions, and the four-stage PPO workflow with its loss functions.
